q: Accessing the k-th node of a singly linked list costs…
why: No indexing: you follow k next-pointers from the head.

q: Inserting a new node right after a node you already have a reference to costs…
When reversing, why save `nxt = cur.next` before `cur.next = prev`?
options: After rewiring, cur.next no longer leads to the rest of the list
why: Overwriting cur.next first would lose the only reference to the remaining nodes.

q: What problem does a dummy node solve?
options: Removing or inserting at the head works like anywhere else
why: The head always has a predecessor (the dummy), so no special case. Return dummy.next.

q: The list is 1 → 2 → 3. After this runs, what does prev point to?
code:
prev, cur = None, head
while cur:
    nxt = cur.next
    cur.next = prev
    prev, cur = cur, nxt
why: Standard reversal: prev ends at the old tail.

q: You must delete a node given only a reference to it, in O(1). Which structure makes this natural?
why: A doubly linked node knows its previous node, so it can unlink itself.
